title: (ICD) Irritant Contact Dermitis
content:
Quick six template



Irritant Contact Dermatitis



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD) is a reaction that takes place when the skin barrier is damaged after it is exposed to a chemical or harmful substance. The most common occurrence of ICD is on the scalp and hands of people who frequently use detergents and water, often through their work (hairdressers).



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) The symptoms of ICD are typically soreness, redness and inflammation of the affected area. The skin may also be cracked, dry and even weeping with fluid in some areas.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Lengthy exposure to detergents or water can remove the natural oils of the outer layers of the skin and cause irritation. In addition, if a damaging agent, such as a chemical, penetrates the protective outer layers of the skin, it comes into contact with the inner cells and tissues. The body reacts by attempting to neutralise the invading agent and repair the damage, resulting in the symptoms of ICD.





Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) ICD is a temporary skin reaction. It usually calms when exposure to the damaging substance is avoided, emollient cream, which makes the skin softer and/or moisturising cream.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) An emollient cream from the pharmacy or if extremely inflamed a topical corticosteroid from the GP

title: Allergic contact dermatitis Quick 6
content:
Quick six template



Allergic contact dermatitis



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Redness  – Heat – Swelling and Pain.  The reaction occurs 12-72 hours after exposure.



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) Sun sensitivity



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Patches of skin that are Itchy, red and blistered – type 4 reaction.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Repeated exposure to small doses of an allergen. Results from an overreaction of the body’s autoimmune system.  Many different allergens can cause this condition.



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) Once the body is sensitised it is for life. 



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) Avoid contact with the substance, refer to GP/Pharmacy for hydrocortisone cream, antihistamine or topical steroids.

title: Alopecia Areata
content:
Quick six template

Alopecia Areata





Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Common cause of patchy hair loss characterised by a well-demarcated shiny patch of non-scarring hair loss. 



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) Short, exclamation hairs at the periphery of the lesion.



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Asymptomatic.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Autoimmune disease that is directed at the hair follicles.



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) 

Unpredictable, normally resolves over time. Nail involvement (pitting). Family history of autoimmune disease. Can occur at any age. 



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) GP can prescribe steroids that are either injected or applied directly (creams or liquids) to the areas where the hair has been shed. Steroids suppress the immune cells that are attacking hair follicles, so hair can regrow.

title: Female Pattern HL Quick 6
content:
Quick six template



Female pattern hair loss



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) FPHL generally presents as a loss of hair volume to the mid-frontal scalp. The parting appears to be getting wider and hair overall could be feeling thinner.



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)Psychological, low self-esteem



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client)Become aware of thinning around hair parting, lack of volume and loss of volume in a ponytail and overall thinning of hair throughout the head



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) It is genetically driven and it involves activation of hair follicle androgen receptors. The miniaturisation of the hair follicle occurs resulting in hair loss. Pattern hair loss (alopecia) is caused by hormones, ageing and genetics. FPHL may also be exacerbated by causes of telogen effluvium such as low ferritin (iron) levels or thyroid dysfunction



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome)There is no cure for FPHL, however, the hair loss process is not constant and usually occurs in fits and bursts. It is not uncommon to have accelerated phases of hair loss for 3–6 months, followed by periods of stability lasting 6–18 months. Without medication, it tends to progress in severity over the next few decades of life.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) 

Treatments would include: Minoxidil, topical steroids from GP, light therapy, wig or hair transplants

title: Folliculitis
content:
Quick six template



Folliculitis 



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Inflammation of the hair follicle.   A skin condition in which hair follicles become inflamed



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)Can occur anyone on hair bearing skin



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Itchiness, burning, and redness within the follicle



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Bacterial infection Folliculitis decalvans.



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome)  Very good. Folliculitis is an easily treated and curable skin condition.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) GP referral

title: Frontal fibrosing alopecia uick six
content:
Quick six template



Frontal Fibrosing Alopecia



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp)Hair loss on the front and sides of the scalp



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)Eyebrows, eyelashes and other body parts



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client)Rash along the hairline and itchy/painful scalp in some cases.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) An autoimmune reaction, genetics or hormones may cause FFA



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) When the hair follicles are destroyed and replaced by scar tissue they cannot regrow.  This means your hair will not grow back.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter)Referral to GP for topical steroids cream/ointment, steroid injections may also be an option in some cases.  Treatment aims to prevent further destruction of your hair follicle but will not be able to make hair grow back that has already been lost.

title: Male pattern hair loss quick 6
content:
Guide to learning the scalp and hair conditions



The Quick 6: Male Pattern Hair Loss (also known as androgenic alopecia)



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Hair loss at the temples or crown of the head, single spot of baldness or hairlines receding to form an “m” shape



Associated signs: (Lesions or signs elsewhere on the body) Psychological – low self-esteem, depression and feelings of unattractiveness.



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by client) Men become aware of scalp hair loss or a receding hairline at any time after puberty, there are usually no symptoms on the scalp.



Aetiology: Cause: client thoughts first (unreliable), Trichologist’s thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) MPHL is caused by a combination of genetic and hormonal factors.  A hormone called DHT (Dihydrotestosterone) causes a change in the hair follicles on the scalp.  The hairs produced by the affected follicles become progressively smaller in diameter, shorter in length and lighter in colour until eventually the follicles shrink completely and stop producing hair.



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) There is no cure, it tends to progress very slowly from several years to decades.  An early onset may lead to quicker progression.  MPHL is inherited from either or both parents.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) Treatment can include topical and oral treatments Minoxidil (slows down the hair loss if taken continuously) and Finasteride (reduces the levels of DHT), also available is wigs/hair pieces, Micro-pigmentation and hair transplants.

title: Sebhorric Dermatits
content:
Quick six template



Seborrheic Dermatitis





Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Red, yellowy, flaky scales. 



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) Nasal folds, eyebrows, armpits and groin



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Inflammation and soreness



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Genetic, yeast infection, stress-related, temperature change (can be worse in winter)



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) Can be managed, but is a long-term, recurring condition.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) From the pharmacy use medicated anti-dandruff shampoo. Sometimes you may need to use a descaling preparation, like coconut oil or salicylic acid, first. Topical steroid cream may be needed from the GP.

title: Telogen effluvium
content:
Quick six template



Telogen Effluvium



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) A sudden loss of hair due to various internal factors. Excesses hair shedding.



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) In rare cases hair loss on the pubic region or eyebrows



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Asymptomatic.



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Telogen effluvium is a clinical sign that signals the existence of an underlying condition.  

The main causes of telogen effluvium are:



Post‐partum hair loss

Febrile illness

Blood loss

Post-­‐operative responses

Endocrine disorders

Drugs and medication

 Metabolic and nutritional disorders

Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) Once treatment of the cause is implemented, the prognosis is normally good and hair growth resumes. 



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) The treatment is the treatment of the cause

title: Traction alopecia Quick 6
content:
Quick six template

Traction alopecia





Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) Areas of hair loss, often to the front and sides of the scalp, that are punctuated with broken hairs. 



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body)



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Inflammation, soreness, stinging or itchiness of the scalp



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Result of repeated or constant pulling on the hair. The pulling force is usually the result of a hairstyling technique, such as a tight ponytail, which exerts an extreme pulling force on the hair and scalp.

Afro-Caribbean styling techniques tend to cause this condition. Examples include:    

Braids 

Cornrows

Dreadlocks

Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) Traction alopecia in many cases is not reversible, although if the treated quickly follicles can recover, or once traction is removed from the hair, then the hair will grow back normally. However, if traction is continued, inflammation becomes more widespread and affects stem cells, which creates scarring, and permanent hair loss.



Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) The tight hairstyles need to be stopped immediately.  If area is inflamed an anti-biotic can be obtained from GP

title: Trichotillosis
content:
Quick six template



Trichotillosis



Signs: (Appearance on the scalp) It is a self-inflicted condition that arises from repeated pulling, twisting or rubbing of strands of hair. The most common site of hair loss is the scalp and hair looks twisted and fragmented.



Associated signs: (Legions or signs elsewhere on the body) Hair loss to Eyelashes and eyebrows



Symptoms: (Sensations experienced by the client) Sense of pleasure or relief after hair is pulled



Aetiology: (Cause, client first (unreliable) Trichologist thoughts after questioning/examination (factually based) Stress-related and compulsive behaviour.   Psychological factors especially in children (stress reduction, emotional regulation, sensory stimulation)



Prognosis: (Prediction of outcome) For most people, the hair pulling ends within 12 months. For others, trichotillomania is a lifelong disorder.

Response: (Advice, treatment, prescription, referral (see the section on producing a referral letter) Seeking treatment for depression, anxiety, or poor self-image often will improve the hair pulling and negative feelings
